(How this works depends on how you configure your policies to handle inputs and\\noutputs.)\\n\\n* The input is evaluated against the configured policies specified in the\\n guardrail. Furthermore, for improved latency, the input is evaluated in parallel\\n for each configured policy.\\n* If the input evaluation results in a guardrail intervention, a configured\\n *blocked message* response is returned and the foundation\\n model inference is discarded.\\n* If the input evaluation succeeds, the model response is then subsequently\\n evaluated against the configured policies in the guardrail.\\n* If the response results in a guardrail intervention or violation, it will be\\n overridden with *pre-configured blocked messaging* or\\n *masking* of the sensitive information based on your\\n policy configuration.\\n* If the response's evaluation succeeds, the response is returned to the\\n application without any\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-how.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Grounding and Retrieval Augmented Generation\",\"context\":\"## Adding guardrails for safety and compliance\\n\\nGrounding enhances accuracy, but production-grade AI demands explicit controls for what the model can and cannot say or do. For more information about scores and thresholds, see Scores and\\n thresholds on this page.\\n* (Optional) For `action`, choose `BLOCK` to block the\\n response and replace it with blocked messaging, or `NONE` to take\\n no action but return detection information. For more information, see Options for handling harmful content detected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.\\n* (Optional) Specify a safeguard tier for your guardrail in the\\n `tierConfig` object within the\\n `contextualGroundingPolicyConfig` object. Options include\\n `STANDARD` and `CLASSIC` tiers. If you omit\\n `tierConfig`, the guardrail uses the `CLASSIC`\\n tier. {"id": "7723140c-bd6b-47be-9414-eac861087d3f", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "**Yes, but don't use the usual fix.** The standard way to cut guardrail latency on streams is asynchronous mode. I wouldn't use it for an app that handles customer account details.

## Why the slowdown happens
In the default **synchronous** mode, the guardrail buffers one or more response chunks and scans them before sending them to the user. That adds delay, but every chunk is checked before the user sees it.

## Why async mode is a poor fit for you
Async mode (`streamProcessingMode: ASYNCHRONOUS`) sends chunks immediately and scans them in the background. The docs state two trade-offs:
- Chunks can reach the user **before** the scan finishes. The guardrail only blocks the chunks that come after it spots a violation. Content that shouldn't be shown could already be on screen.
- **Sensitive information masking isn't supported in async mode.** If you use PII masking on account details, async would turn it off.

That weakens your protection, so I'd rule it out.

## Options that keep protection
These are my suggestions. I haven't checked them against your guardrail, and the docs I pulled don't give latency numbers for them.

1. **Trim the guardrail to the policies you need.** Each policy (content filters, denied topics, word filters, PII filters, contextual grounding) adds evaluation work. Review the guardrail for policies that duplicate each other or don't apply to a chat app. Contextual grounding checks are worth a close look if you don't need them.
2. **Compare safeguard tiers.** Some policies offer Classic and Standard tiers. Measure both on your own traffic before changing anything. Standard tier needs cross-Region inference, which may matter for your data-residency rules.
3. **Move input checks off the streaming path.** The docs say input is evaluated in parallel across policies and before model inference. If your system prompt and retrieved context are large, mark only the user-supplied part for evaluation using input tagging. This shrinks the input scan without touching output checks.
4. **Hide the buffering in the UI.** Show a typing indicator and render in small steps. Sync buffering is bursty, so smoothing it on the client often fixes the perceived slowness.
5. **Measure before and after.** Compare time-to-first-token and total stream time with and without the guardrail attached. Turn on the guardrail trace to see which policies intervene or run slowly. That tells you what's worth changing.

## If you still want async
It could be acceptable if the protection that matters most for account details is enforced **outside** the stream. For example, don't put raw account data in the model's context, or filter it deterministically in your own code before the model sees it. I'd treat that as a security design decision to review with your security team, not a quick tuning change.

If you tell me whether you're using `ConverseStream` or `InvokeModelWithResponseStream`, and which policies are on the guardrail, I can narrow this down. I can also look at your guardrail configuration and Bedrock latency metrics in the account if you want.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
